Drowning Girl

Roy Lichtenstein’s romance-comic close-up: a crying woman in a stylized wave, with a thought balloon that reads “I DON’T CARE! I’D RATHER SINK — THAN CALL BRAD FOR HELP!”

Source
Roy Lichtenstein: A Catalogue Raisonné, Drowning Girl (RLCR 761)
Creator
Roy Lichtenstein
Made
1963
Style
Pop art (agent-proposed, not yet reviewed by a person)
Moods
Melodramatic, graphic, ironic
Evidence
Downloaded and inspected the catalogue raisonné image of the Museum of Modern Art’s painting, MoMA 685.1971 (1180 × 1200 px), in a scratchpad. MoMA’s own page blocks scripts. No image is stored.
Reviewed
28 September 2026
Rights
Link and metadata only. License: unverified. Rights policy

Context

The catalogue raisonné gives acrylic, oil, and graphite pencil on canvas, 171.8 × 169.5 cm, and the source as Secret Hearts #83 (November 1962). The Museum of Modern Art acquired it in December 1971 (685.1971). RLCR 761.

It was shown in Lichtenstein’s September–October 1963 exhibition at the Leo Castelli Gallery, the show announced by the Crak! poster. RLCR 761.

Wikipedia reports that the work also borrows from Hokusai’s The Great Wave off Kanagawa. Wikipedia.

Observed

  • The face, hand, and arm are filled with fine red dots on white; the lips are flat pink with a black outline.
  • The hair is solid ultramarine blue with black strands. No blue dots appear in the hair.
  • The water is a pattern of heavy black curls and white foam shapes on a pale blue dot field.
  • A white thought balloon with a scalloped outline and three small bubbles fills the upper left. It holds four lines of black hand-lettered capitals.
  • Tears are drawn as white drops with black outlines.
  • Black outlines vary from thick to very thick. There are no gradients or modeled shadows.

Why it belongs

The painting shows the romance branch of the idiom: close-up faces, a limited palette of dot-red skin and one solid primary, and text in a balloon, not a caption box.

Large black shapes carry as much of the design as the outlines do. The style is not only outline plus fill; solid black areas give it weight.

Borrow

Use a scalloped thought balloon for a quote or testimonial, with small trailing bubbles.

Tint large areas with a pale dot field and reserve one strong solid color for the focal shape.
